questions.prompt: What is 'documentation debt,' as this course defines it?
options: The accumulating cost of undocumented or stale decisions, paid later by whoever has to reconstruct them
The monetary cost of buying diagramming software licenses
A penalty Salesforce applies to orgs without written architecture
The time it takes to read a design document end to end
questions.explain: Like technical debt, documentation debt is the gap between the fast path (skip writing it down) and the durable path (document it) — the interest on that gap is paid later by whoever has to reverse-engineer the design.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B describes a real cost (software licensing) but not the one this course calls documentation debt — that term specifically names the cost of undocumented or stale decisions, not tooling spend.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is one of the five standard sections of an architecture decision record (ADR)?
options: Lifeline
Status — tracking whether a decision is Proposed, Accepted, or Superseded
Cardinality
Activation bar
questions.explain: The five standard ADR sections are Title, Status, Context, Decision, and Consequences. Status is the one field expected to change after the record is first written.
questions.distractorExplain: Lifeline is a sequence-diagram element (Lesson 5), not an ADR section — it's easy to confuse diagram notation terms with document-section names, but they're different kinds of artifact.

questions.prompt: On a crow's-foot ERD, a line between Account and Opportunity shows a single tick at the Account end and a crow's foot at the Opportunity end. What does this mean?
options: Many Accounts relate to many Opportunities
One Account relates to many Opportunities, and each Opportunity relates to exactly one Account
One Account relates to exactly one Opportunity
Opportunities cannot be related to Accounts
questions.explain: A single tick means 'one' and a crow's foot means 'many' — one Account can have many Opportunities, and each Opportunity belongs to exactly one Account, matching a standard Salesforce lookup.

questions.prompt: Match each diagram type to the specific question it answers.
right: What is this system, and what external actors/systems does it touch?
As data moves through a process, what transforms and stores it?
In what exact order do messages happen during one transaction?
What entities exist and how are they related?
questions.explain: Each diagram type exists at a different zoom level and answers a different question: context (boundary), DFD (structure of movement), sequence (exact order/timing), ERD (data shape).

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: once an ADR is accepted, if a later team reverses the decision, the correct fix is to write a new ADR and mark the old one's status as ________ by the new ADR.
questions.explain: ADRs are treated as an immutable log — the old record's content stays as written, but its status is updated to show it has been superseded by the new ADR.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about data-flow diagram (DFD) notation.
options: A DFD never connects two data stores directly to each other — data always moves through a process
An external entity can be a person, a role, or another system outside the process being described
A DFD specifies the exact timing and order of events, the same way a sequence diagram does
Leveling lets the same process be shown at increasing levels of detail, from a context-level bubble down to Level 1
A data store is where a process transforms data, rather than where data is held at rest
questions.explain: DFDs never connect two data stores or two external entities directly; external entities are people, roles, or outside systems; leveling moves from a context bubble to Level 0 to Level 1. A DFD is deliberately silent on timing (that's a sequence diagram's job), and a data store holds data at rest rather than transforming it.

questions.prompt: Put these data-flow-diagram leveling stages in order, from the widest view to the most detailed.
items: Context-level DFD (the entire process as one bubble)
Level 1 DFD (a complex sub-process exploded further)
questions.explain: Leveling starts with a single context-level bubble, explodes it into major sub-processes at Level 0, and explodes any still-complex sub-process further at Level 1 — each level adding more detail than the one above it.

questions.prompt: An integration's exact call order involves a synchronous Apex callout, a retry on timeout, and a fallback response. Which SDD section should this integration's detail live in, and what diagram often accompanies it?
options: The executive summary; no diagram is needed
The assumptions and open items section; a data-flow diagram
The integration design section; a sequence diagram, since the order and timing of calls is complex enough that prose alone could be read more than one way
The non-functional requirements section; no diagram at all
questions.explain: Integration design is the SDD section for pattern, auth, mapping, and error handling, and a sequence diagram earns its place when order and timing are complex enough that prose alone would be ambiguous.

questions.prompt: Match each audience to the real question their documentation needs to answer.
right: Is this safe to invest in, and what could still go wrong?
What exactly do I need to build, and what has already been decided?
When something breaks, what do I check first?
Did this architect consider the realistic alternatives, and can they defend the trade-offs?
questions.explain: Each audience reads at a different altitude: an executive wants investment risk, a developer wants build detail and prior decisions, an admin wants operational steps, and a review panel wants to see the reasoning defended.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a good architecture executive summary is disciplined to fit on ________ page, answering what problem is being solved, what's recommended, what it costs, and what risk remains.
questions.explain: The one-page constraint is a feature, not a limitation — it forces real clarity, since a long summary gets skimmed rather than read.

questions.prompt: A team's documentation template requires every SDD to fully fill in all nine sections, even for a tiny internal tool with no integrations. What failure mode does this risk, per this course?
options: Under-templating, since the template doesn't have enough sections
No failure — every section must always be filled in completely regardless of relevance
Documentation rot, since the template itself is now out of date
Over-templating — box-ticking irrelevant sections, producing a longer document that buries what actually matters
questions.explain: Over-templating happens when a rigid template forces content into sections that don't apply — the fix is marking a section 'Not applicable' with a one-sentence reason, not forcing it to be filled in regardless of relevance.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the trade-off between GUI diagramming tools and diagram-as-code tools.
options: GUI tools (Lucidchart, diagrams.net, Visio) are strong for fast, polished visual layout
Diagram-as-code tools (Mermaid, PlantUML) represent a diagram as text, which can be versioned and diffed in Git
A binary GUI-tool diagram file diffs cleanly line by line in a pull request, the same as a text file
Diagram-as-code tools generally trade some visual polish and fine-grained layout control for that diffability
No team should ever use a GUI diagramming tool for official architecture documentation
questions.explain: GUI tools are strong for fast, polished manual layout; diagram-as-code tools trade some of that polish for text-based version control and diffability. A binary GUI file does NOT diff cleanly line by line — that's exactly the gap diagram-as-code fills.

questions.prompt: A diagram shows a plain line between two Salesforce objects with no legend. Why is this a problem, per this course's standards?
options: Plain lines are always forbidden on any diagram
Without a legend, a reader can't tell whether the line is a lookup or a master-detail relationship — a distinction with real cascading-delete and roll-up-summary consequences
It means the diagram was drawn in Schema Builder
It means the relationship is necessarily many-to-many
questions.explain: A legend is what turns an ambiguous line into an unambiguous one — without it, a plain relationship line can't tell a reader whether cascading delete and roll-up summaries apply.

questions.prompt: A custom Task__c object uses a lookup (not master-detail) relationship to Project__c, specifically so Task records survive if a Project is deleted and recreated. What question did this decision answer?
options: Which relationship type is alphabetically first in Setup
Whether the object is standard or custom
What should happen to the child record if the parent is deleted — should it be destroyed along with the parent, or should it survive?
Which relationship type requires less configuration effort
questions.explain: The real question behind lookup vs. master-detail is what should happen to the child on parent deletion — Task__c needed to survive a Project's deletion and recreation, so lookup (no cascading delete) was the deliberate choice.

questions.prompt: Match each Salesforce sharing-model layer to what it controls.
right: The baseline record-level access before any other mechanism opens it back up
Criteria- or ownership-based rules that open access beyond OWD and role hierarchy for specific groups
Object- and field-level CRUD permissions, independent of record-level sharing
Visibility and editability of a specific field, which can restrict access even with full object/record access
questions.explain: OWD sets the baseline; sharing rules open access beyond it for specific groups; permission sets/profiles govern CRUD independent of record sharing; field-level security can restrict a specific field even when object and record access are otherwise granted.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: written documentation quietly falling out of sync with the real system over time is called documentation ________.
questions.explain: Documentation rot is structural, not a discipline failure — nothing in a typical change process automatically updates documentation, so without a deliberate review process, rot is the default outcome of ordinary change.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about documenting a Salesforce integration's pattern choice.
options: A fire-and-forget pattern needs documentation of how the publisher would ever learn about a downstream failure, since it doesn't wait for a response by design
A batch pattern's documentation should address what happens when a batch partially succeeds
Pattern choice has no effect on what the error-handling section needs to cover
An event-driven pattern built on Platform Events needs documentation of subscriber behavior if a subscriber is offline when an event publishes
Every integration, regardless of pattern, should use identical error-handling documentation
questions.explain: Pattern choice drives exactly what error handling needs to address: fire-and-forget needs a failure-detection story, batch needs a partial-success story, and event-driven needs an offline-subscriber story — these are not interchangeable or identical across patterns.

questions.prompt: Put these Salesforce sharing-model layers in the order this course says they apply, from the baseline to the most specific override.
questions.explain: OWD sets the baseline access before anything else applies; role hierarchy opens access down the management chain; sharing rules open further access to specific groups; field-level security is the final, most specific layer, able to restrict a field even when the record is otherwise visible.

questions.prompt: In a case-study mock review, a question exposes a place in the documentation that can't be answered from what's already written. What does this course say that means?
options: The reviewer's question was unfair and out of scope
The entire documentation set must be discarded and rewritten from scratch
The mock review exercise itself is invalid
That specific gap is a real gap in the design's reasoning, not just a writing problem, and the relevant section should be fixed
questions.explain: An unanswerable question usually means a decision was never actually worked through, not just poorly written down — the fix is targeted (update the relevant section), not a full rewrite or a dismissal of the question.

questions.prompt: A team reviews documentation only 'whenever someone has time.' What problem does this course say that causes?
options: Review happens inconsistently or not at all, which is exactly how documentation rot accumulates unchecked
Nothing — review timing doesn't affect documentation quality
It guarantees release-triggered review happens reliably
It is the Salesforce-recommended review cadence
questions.explain: Without a defined trigger (release-triggered or scheduled periodic review), review happens only opportunistically, which doesn't reliably catch the rot that accumulates from ordinary, legitimate change over time.
